also: did you have a good night?

terms.grammar: perfect of quiēscō, quiēscere, quiēvī, quiētum, rest, sleep
evidence: Plin. Ep. 3.16: Bene quiēvit, libenter cibum sūmpsit.
Plaut. Merc. 370: poste hāc nocte nōn quiēvī satis meā ex sententiā.
terms.comment: The verb of a night’s rest is quiēscere (Lewis & Short: “to rest, sleep”). Pliny tells how Arria answered her sick husband each time he asked after their son, who had in fact died: Bene quiēvit, libenter cibum sūmpsit. In Plautus a young man explains his pale face to his father: nōn quiēvī satis meā ex sententiā, I didn’t sleep as well as I’d have liked. The answer repeats the verb: Bene quiēvī, or Nōn satis quiēvī.

evidence: Publil. Syr.: Bene dormit, quī nōn sentit quam male dormiat.
terms.comment: The same question with the everyday verb dormīre; bene dormīre is in Publilius.

phrases.english: Good morning, my boy. Did you sleep well?

phrases.latin: Nōn satis quiēvī; somnium mē terruit.
phrases.english: I didn’t sleep well; a dream frightened me.
He has slept well, and eaten with an appetite.

phrases.latin: poste hāc nocte nōn quiēvī satis meā ex sententiā.
phrases.english: and then last night I didn’t sleep as well as I’d have liked.

sources: Lewis & Short: quiesco · Lewis & Short: dormio
